title: The seven books (the deuterocanon)
hookLine: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1–2 Maccabees are in Catholic Bibles; many Protestants call them the Apocrypha
last: ALL YE WORKS, BLESS THE LORD.

cards: Put a Catholic Bible and a Protestant Bible side by side and count the books. The Catholic one has seventy-three: forty-six in the Old Testament and twenty-seven in the New, as the Catechism counts them.
The Protestant one will usually have sixty-six; the Westminster Confession, a Protestant statement of faith, lists them by name. The New Testaments match exactly.

The difference is all in the Old Testament: seven books, plus extra passages in Esther and Daniel, like yesterday's song from the furnace. Same faith in Christ, same Gospels, and a different-sized shelf.

teach.b: The seven are Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and First and Second Maccabees. Catholics call them deuterocanonical.
Canon comes from the Greek kanon, a straight rod for measuring, and so a rule, and so the list of books measured as scripture. Deutero means second.
Not second-rate: their place in the list was settled later, after some discussion. Catholics hold them to be inspired scripture, fully. The history, as plainly as possible.

Before Jesus, Jews in the Greek-speaking world used a Greek translation of their scriptures, the Septuagint, and its collections included these books. The early Church, mostly Greek-speaking, read that Bible.
North African councils around the year 400 list them as scripture. Saint Jerome, translating from the Hebrew, had doubts and set them in a separate category, though he translated some anyway.
In his German Bible, Martin Luther gathered them into a section between the Testaments, calling them Apocrypha: not held equal to scripture, but useful and good to read.
The Council of Trent in 1546 answered by defining the Catholic canon with all seven included.

The first King James Bible printed them too, between the Testaments; later printings could leave them out. Today the Jewish Bible doesn't include them. The Orthodox churches include them and a few more.
Protestant confessions like Westminster don't count them as scripture; the Church of England's Articles say they are read for example of life, but not to establish doctrine.
In a Catholic Bible they sit right in among the others. Over the next week, this path opens four of them.

how: Catholics hear readings from the deuterocanonical books at Mass, at weddings (Tobit), funerals (Wisdom) and in the prayers for the dead (2 Maccabees), the same as any other book of scripture.

games.q: you're a reader in the early Church, and your Bible is the Greek one. it includes Tobit, Judith, Wisdom and Maccabees. what do you do with them?

games.why: the Greek Bible the early Church read included them, and North African councils around 400 listed them as scripture.

practice: If you have a Catholic Bible nearby, open the contents: Tobit comes after Nehemiah, which the Douay calls Second Esdras, with Judith next; read just its first verse.
If not, picture the shelf, forty-six books, seven you may never have opened. If you pray, ask for a little curiosity about the pages you've never read.

wordCard.voice: Deuterocanonical. The seven Old Testament books, and parts of Esther and Daniel, whose place in the canon was settled later; Catholics receive them as scripture. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a straight rod for measuring, a rule; the canon is the list of books measured as scripture.

carryVoice: Your line: the books between. Seven books, and a longer shelf than you thought. See you tomorrow.
